http.q: Why does the browser send a DNS query before the HTTP request?
options: Packets are addressed by IP, not by name
HTTP requires DNS to encrypt the request
The server only accepts requests after a DNS check
http.why: IP packets need an address; DNS turns www.example.com into 203.0.113.10.

http.q: Which packet finishes the TCP three-way handshake?
http.why: SYN, SYN-ACK, then the client's ACK; only then can data flow.

http.q: The 12.2 KB page arrives as 9 TCP segments because…
options: each segment carries at most the MSS of 1,460 bytes
HTTP splits every response into 9 parts
http.why: TCP cuts the stream into segments no larger than the maximum segment size.

https.q: What can someone on the network still read in an HTTPS visit?
options: The server name in the Client Hello (SNI)
https.why: Without Encrypted Client Hello, the SNI is sent in clear text; everything after the handshake is encrypted.

https.q: What does the server's certificate prove?
options: That the server controls the name www.example.com
That the page has no malware
That DNS was not tampered with
https.why: A trusted CA signed a binding between the name and the server's public key.

https.q: Compared with HTTP, how many extra round trips before the GET?
https.why: TLS 1.3 needs one round trip after the TCP handshake before application data.

http3.q: Why must a client QUIC Initial datagram be at least 1,200 bytes?
options: So the server can't be used to amplify attacks
Because UDP has a minimum size
To make room for the HTML
http3.why: The server may send at most three times what it received until the address is verified.

http3.q: When does the GET leave in HTTP/3?
options: With the client's Finished, after one round trip
After a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake
Only after the server sends HANDSHAKE_DONE
http3.why: QUIC merges transport and TLS handshakes, so the request goes after one round trip.

http3.q: If one datagram of a response is lost, QUIC…
options: delays only the stream that datagram belonged to
stops every stream until it's resent
http3.why: QUIC orders data per stream, avoiding TCP's head-of-line blocking across streams.

websocket.q: How does a WebSocket connection begin?
options: As an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket
websocket.why: The server answers 101 Switching Protocols and the connection then carries WebSocket frames.

options: Frames from the browser to the server
websocket.why: Client-to-server frames carry a 4-byte masking key; server frames don't.

websocket.q: What is the ping/pong exchange for?
options: Keeping idle connections alive and detecting dead peers
websocket.why: A peer must answer a ping with a pong.

tcp.q: How does the laptop tell the server a segment is missing?
tcp.why: The ACK keeps asking for the gap, while SACK reports what arrived after it.
With SACK, only the gap is retransmitted.

tcp.q: Why does every byte have a sequence number?
options: So the receiver can order data and spot gaps
tcp.why: Sequence and acknowledgment numbers make TCP reliable and ordered.

udp.q: What happens to the lost voice datagram?
udp.why: UDP has no acknowledgments; the app decides how to cope.

udp.q: Why is UDP a good fit for live voice?
options: A late packet is useless, so waiting for resends would hurt more
udp.why: Real-time audio prefers fresh data over complete data.

udp.q: How big is a UDP header?
udp.why: Source port, destination port, length and checksum: 2 bytes each.

ip.q: How does the laptop find the router's MAC address?
ip.why: ARP maps an IPv4 address on the local network to a MAC address.

ip.q: What changes when the packet passes through NAT?
ip.why: The router rewrites 192.168.1.10:52344 to its public address 198.51.100.7:40112.

ip.q: Why does the TTL drop from 128 to 127?
options: Each router decrements it by one
ip.why: TTL limits how many hops a packet can travel.

ipv6.q: Which protocol replaces ARP in IPv6?
ipv6.why: Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement messages map addresses to MACs.

ipv6.q: Where does the laptop's global address come from?
options: The advertised prefix plus its own interface ID (SLAAC)
ipv6.why: The Router Advertisement supplies the 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 prefix. The laptop combines it with its interface identifier.

ipv6.q: Why does the laptop send a Neighbor Solicitation for its own address?
options: To check nobody else is using it (DAD)
ipv6.why: Duplicate Address Detection runs before any address is used.

ethernet.q: What does a switch do with a frame to an unknown MAC?
options: Floods it out of every other port
ethernet.why: Unknown and broadcast destinations are flooded; known ones go to one port.

ethernet.q: How does the switch learn where a device is?
options: From the source MAC of frames it receives
ethernet.why: Each received frame teaches it source MAC → port.

ethernet.q: Sending to 8.8.8.8, the Ethernet destination is…
ethernet.why: Ethernet only reaches the next hop; IP carries the final destination.

wifi.q: Does WPA2 send the Wi-Fi password in the four-way handshake?
options: No; the peers prove that they derived matching keys
Only when the password is short
wifi.why: The peers exchange nonces and authentication tags. They derive keys from the shared secret without sending that secret.

options: The pairwise key (PTK) and the group key (GTK)
wifi.why: Nonces plus the PMK give the PTK; message 3 delivers the GTK.

wifi.q: Which fields of an encrypted data frame are still visible?
options: The MAC addresses in the 802.11 header
wifi.why: CCMP encrypts the payload, not the link-layer header.

dns.q: Which server first points the resolver to .com?
dns.why: Root servers answer with a referral to the .com servers.

dns.q: What does 'recursion desired' ask the resolver to do?
options: Do the whole lookup and return the final answer
dns.why: The laptop asks one question; the resolver walks the hierarchy.

dns.q: Why will the next lookup be faster?
options: The resolver caches the answer for its TTL
The root server remembers the laptop
dns.why: Cached answers are reused until their TTL expires.

doh.q: With DoH, who can read the DNS question?
doh.why: The query travels inside HTTPS to the resolver.

doh.q: Why does this DoH connection use TCP port 443?
options: It carries DNS messages inside HTTPS
The DNS answer chooses that port
doh.why: DoH uses an HTTPS connection to the resolver. The DNS message is application data protected by TLS.

doh.q: What can an observer read in the first ordinary DNS exchange?
options: The queried name and the returned IP address
doh.why: The first query and response are plain DNS over UDP. The later DoH messages hide their DNS contents inside TLS.

dhcp.q: Why is the Discover sent from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255?
options: The laptop has no address yet and doesn't know the server
dhcp.why: Broadcast reaches every device on the segment, including the DHCP server.

dhcp.q: What does the Request message do?
dhcp.why: Broadcasting the Request tells other servers their offers were declined.

dhcp.q: When does the laptop renew its lease?
dhcp.why: Renewal (T1) starts at 50% of the lease time.

icmp.q: What does a router send when a packet's TTL reaches zero?
icmp.why: Traceroute uses these replies to name each hop.

icmp.q: How does traceroute discover the path?
icmp.why: Each probe expires one hop further.

options: The round-trip time to a host
icmp.why: Echo request out, echo reply back.

smtp.q: How does the sending server find the recipient's mail server?
smtp.why: MX records name the mail servers for a domain.

options: Upgrades a plain connection on port 25 to TLS
smtp.why: The session begins in plain text and switches to TLS.

smtp.q: Which port does the laptop use to submit mail in this lesson?

pop3.q: When is a message deleted from the server in POP3?
pop3.why: DELE marks it; the deletion happens when the session ends with QUIT.

options: Number of messages and total size

pop3.q: Why can POP3 make mail disappear from other devices?
options: It downloads and usually deletes from the server
pop3.why: POP3 is designed for one device taking the mail.

imap.q: Why do IMAP commands start with tags like a1, a2?
imap.why: Tagged responses let several commands be in flight.

options: Lets the server push new-mail notifications
imap.why: The client waits; the server reports changes as they happen.

options: On the server, so every device sees it
imap.why: IMAP keeps state on the server.

ftp.q: Why does FTP open a second TCP connection?
options: Files travel on a separate data connection
ftp.why: Commands use port 21; data uses the port named by PASV.

ftp.q: Which risk does this lesson show?
options: The password crosses the network in clear text
ftp.why: PASS secret is readable by anyone on the path.

ftp.q: How does the server name the data port in passive mode?

ssh.q: How does the laptop log in without sending a secret?
options: It signs the session with its private key
It sends its public key only
ssh.why: The server verifies the signature with the authorized public key.

ssh.q: What does the host key protect against?
ssh.why: The client checks the server's host key against known_hosts.

ssh.q: Which messages are still readable on the wire?
options: The version banners and algorithm lists

tls.q: How many round trips does a TLS 1.3 full handshake take?
tls.why: Client Hello out, server flight back, then application data.

tls.q: What carries the key share in TLS 1.3?
options: The Client Hello and Server Hello
tls.why: Key shares travel in the hellos, so keys exist after one round trip.

options: An alert telling the peer no more data will follow
tls.why: It prevents truncation attacks before TCP closes.

webrtc.q: What does the STUN reply tell the browser?
options: The public address and port seen by the STUN server
webrtc.why: The XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS describes how this browser’s traffic appears outside its local network. ICE can use that candidate while testing a route to the peer.

webrtc.q: Why does the call exchange DTLS messages before sending media?
options: To establish authenticated key material for protected media
To download the entire call in advance
To replace every UDP packet with TCP
webrtc.why: DTLS negotiates security over datagrams. The resulting key material protects the media exchange shown next.

webrtc.q: Which packets carry the protected audio and video?
webrtc.why: Signaling arranges the call and STUN tests connectivity. SRTP carries the protected media, using sequence numbers and timestamps for playback.

bgp.q: Which transport does this BGP session use?
bgp.why: The routers establish a TCP connection before exchanging BGP OPEN messages. This capture shows destination port 179.

bgp.q: What does the UPDATE for 203.0.113.0/24 announce?
options: Reachability information for that network prefix
An address lease for one laptop
bgp.why: BGP advertises prefixes and their path attributes. Neighboring networks can use that information when selecting a route.

bgp.q: What does a route withdrawal tell a neighbor?
options: The previously advertised route is no longer available through this announcement
The destination server has sent an HTTP error
bgp.why: A withdrawal removes an advertised route from consideration. A router may select another available route or lose reachability to that prefix.

dnssec.q: What does the RRSIG in a signed DNS answer provide?
options: A signature that a validator can check
Encryption of the entire DNS exchange
An automatic guarantee that the website is safe
dnssec.why: DNSSEC lets a resolver authenticate signed DNS data and detect modifications. It does not conceal the query or assess the website’s content.

dnssec.q: Why does the resolver request DNSKEY records?
options: To obtain the zone’s public validation keys
To obtain the server’s private signing key
To change the laptop’s MAC address
dnssec.why: DNSKEY records publish the keys used when checking signatures for the zone. Public keys are safe to distribute; the signing private key stays with the operator.

dnssec.q: How does the parent zone help validate a child zone?
options: Its signed DS record identifies a child key
It sends the child’s private key
It encrypts the laptop’s Ethernet frame
It converts the answer to an MX record
dnssec.why: A validated DS record links the parent’s trust chain to a child DNSKEY. The resolver can then validate the child’s signed data.

ntp.q: What is the purpose of this NTP exchange?
options: Estimate the difference between the client’s clock and a time source
Assign the client an IP address
ntp.why: The client sends a timing request and receives timestamps from a server. These observations help estimate clock offset and network delay.

ntp.q: Why are timestamps from both sides useful?
options: They help separate clock offset from time spent in transit
They make every network path perfectly symmetric
They eliminate all clock error after one packet
ntp.why: NTP uses a set of timestamps around the exchange to estimate delay and offset. Unequal path delays and measurement noise can still affect the result.

ntp.q: Why may a clock be adjusted gradually?
options: To avoid an abrupt jump in time used by applications
To change the server’s port number
To send a larger DNS answer
ntp.why: Small corrections can be applied by changing the clock’s rate for a while. This reduces disruption for software that relies on time moving forward predictably.

wpa3.q: What is SAE proving during WPA3-Personal authentication?
options: That each peer knows the shared password without sending it
That the access point owns an HTTPS certificate
That DNS has assigned a public IP address
wpa3.why: SAE uses commit and confirm exchanges to establish a shared secret and prove knowledge of the password. The password itself is not a field sent over the air.

wpa3.q: What follows the SAE commit messages?
wpa3.why: The confirm exchange checks that both peers derived matching authentication state. Association and the four-way handshake follow in this capture.

wpa3.q: Why is there still a four-way handshake after SAE?
options: To establish and install the keys used to protect link traffic
To send the password in plain text
To ask a DNS resolver for the SSID
To assign a TCP sequence number
wpa3.why: Successful SAE establishes key material. The later EAPOL exchange derives and installs the traffic keys needed for protected Wi-Fi frames.

radius.q: Who forwards the authentication conversation to RADIUS?
options: The network access device, such as the access point
radius.why: The access point relays authentication information between the station and the authentication server. It controls access according to the result.

radius.q: What is EAP-TLS using to authenticate in this lesson?
radius.why: EAP-TLS carries a TLS authentication exchange inside EAP. Certificates allow the parties to verify identity rather than relying only on a shared Wi-Fi password.

options: The authentication server has accepted this access request
Every later network packet is automatically safe
The browser has received an HTML page
radius.why: Access-Accept reports the server’s authorization decision and may include session attributes. The access device then completes the local access setup.

portal.q: Why does the device request a connectivity-check page?
options: To test whether ordinary internet access is available
To download a certificate private key
To change the Wi-Fi radio channel
portal.why: The operating system expects a recognizable response from a known connectivity endpoint. A redirect or unexpected body can indicate a captive portal.

portal.q: What does the first HTTP 302 response do?
options: Redirect the connectivity check toward the portal
portal.why: An HTTP redirect tells the client to fetch another location. Here it leads toward the network’s login or terms page.

portal.q: What indicates that access is available after accepting the terms?
options: The later connectivity check receives the expected normal response
The device changes its Ethernet manufacturer
The TCP port becomes a Wi-Fi password
portal.why: The device repeats its connectivity check after the portal exchange. The ordinary successful response indicates that the check is no longer being redirected.

smb.q: Which service port does this file-sharing connection use?
smb.why: The initial TCP handshake targets port 445. The endpoints then negotiate the SMB protocol carried over that connection.

options: A shared resource such as the Documents share
smb.why: An SMB tree represents a connection to a shared resource. Once connected, the client can issue file operations within that share.

smb.q: Why is the SMB read response shown as many TCP segments?
options: The requested file data is larger than one transport segment
Every segment contains a different password
SMB requires one connection per byte
smb.why: The read returns a large application message. TCP transports it across multiple segments while presenting an ordered byte stream to SMB.

proxy.q: Why does the browser send the whole URL to the HTTP proxy?
options: The proxy needs the destination authority as well as the resource path
The URL is an Ethernet address
The browser has already downloaded the response
A proxy cannot open another TCP connection
proxy.why: An HTTP forward proxy receives an absolute-form target for this request. It can use the target to connect to the origin and forward the request.

proxy.q: What is the purpose of CONNECT in this exchange?
options: Ask the proxy to establish a tunnel to the named host and port
proxy.why: After the proxy reports that the connection is established, bytes can pass through the tunnel. The browser can negotiate TLS with the destination through it.

proxy.q: Who initiates the TLS Client Hello inside the tunnel?
proxy.why: The proxy forwards the tunneled byte stream. The Client Hello shown here belongs to the browser’s TLS conversation with the destination.

socks.q: What does the SOCKS5 greeting negotiate?
options: An authentication method supported by the client and proxy
socks.why: The client lists supported methods and the proxy selects one. This example chooses the no-authentication method.

socks.q: What information does the SOCKS CONNECT request supply?
socks.why: SOCKS asks the proxy to open a transport connection to the requested destination. The application protocol can then pass through that connection.

socks.q: Does selecting no SOCKS authentication also disable TLS to the website?
options: No; the tunneled application can still negotiate TLS
Yes; TLS cannot travel through a proxy
Yes; the proxy replaces all packets with DNS
No, because SOCKS automatically encrypts every byte itself
socks.why: SOCKS authentication and destination TLS are separate mechanisms. This capture shows a TLS Client Hello after the SOCKS connection succeeds.

reverse.q: Where does the browser-facing TLS connection terminate in this lesson?
options: At the laptop’s default gateway only
reverse.why: The reverse proxy acts as the browser’s TLS endpoint. It can read the decrypted request before forwarding it to the backend.

reverse.q: How is the backend request carried in this example?
options: As ordinary HTTP on the backend connection
As a new DNS resource record
As the browser’s original encrypted TLS record
reverse.why: The frontend TLS session and backend connection are separate. This example forwards plain HTTP internally; other deployments can use encrypted backend transport.

reverse.q: What does the browser receive when the backend answers?
options: A response protected by the frontend TLS session
An unencrypted Ethernet broadcast of the page
reverse.why: The reverse proxy receives the backend response and sends the result through its browser-facing TLS connection. The browser sees protected application data.

wireguard.q: What do the first WireGuard messages establish?
options: An authenticated session with keys for tunnel traffic
A DHCP lease for every internet host
wireguard.why: WireGuard peers use the handshake to authenticate and establish traffic keys. Later transport messages protect packets sent through the tunnel.

wireguard.q: What is inside a WireGuard transport message?
options: A BGP routing table in every packet
An HTTP status line with no network header
wireguard.why: The tunnel protects an inner packet while outer network headers carry the transport message to the peer. The receiving peer decrypts it before forwarding.

wireguard.q: Why send an otherwise empty keepalive?
options: To preserve useful network state such as a NAT mapping
To download the entire website again
To publish the peer’s private key
wireguard.why: A small authenticated keepalive can keep a path’s state from expiring during idle periods. It does not carry a user application payload.

options: Initial cryptographic parameters and key-exchange material
A DNS alias for the router
ipsec.why: The peers first establish the cryptographic groundwork for IKE. The later authenticated exchange verifies identities and negotiates traffic protection.

ipsec.q: What is the role of IKE_AUTH?
options: Authenticate the peers and establish the protected traffic association
ipsec.why: IKE_AUTH binds the negotiation to authenticated identities and establishes the association used for protected traffic. Its sensitive exchange is protected after the initial setup.

ipsec.q: Which packets carry the protected tunneled traffic here?
ipsec.why: ESP protects the traffic governed by the IPsec association. Its security parameters index identifies the receiving association without exposing the protected application bytes.

modbus.q: Which operation does function code 3 request?
modbus.why: The query identifies a unit and a range of holding registers. The response returns the requested register values when the operation succeeds.

modbus.q: What does function code 6 do in this exchange?
modbus.why: The write request supplies a register address and a value. The successful response echoes the operation so the client can match the result to its request.

modbus.q: What does the exception response report?
options: The requested data address is not valid for this operation
modbus.why: Modbus exceptions report application-level errors. This response uses the exception form of the function code and the illegal-data-address exception value.
